analysis.one_liner: Lets wheelchair owners and independent shops repair powered wheelchairs without manufacturer locks.
analysis.headline: A bill to give wheelchair users and independent repair shops the tools and parts to fix powered wheelchairs was introduced and referred to two House committees, where it awaits action.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require companies that make powered wheelchairs and other mobility devices to sell parts, manuals, diagnostic software, and repair tools to independent repair shops and device owners on the same terms they give their own authorized dealers. It would also change copyright law so that bypassing software locks to diagnose, maintain, or repair a mobility device is not illegal. The Federal Trade Commission and state attorneys general could enforce the rules.
analysis.who_benefits: People who use powered wheelchairs or exoskeletons, who would no longer have to rely solely on the manufacturer or its authorized dealers for repairs. Independent repair shops would gain access to parts, manuals, diagnostic software, and lock-reset tools needed to fix devices, and device owners would gain the right to repair their own equipment. Rural users far from an authorized dealer would likely see the biggest practical change, since they could use any local shop.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Wheelchair users and independent repair shops

how_it_helps.text: The bill requires manufacturers to make documentation, parts, embedded software, firmware, and repair tools available to independent repair providers and owners on fair and reasonable terms, meaning terms at least as good as those given to their own authorized dealers [S2].

It adds an exception to copyright law so that circumventing a technological lock for the diagnosis, maintenance, or repair of a powered mobility device is not a violation, and so that selling tools or parts for that purpose is not illegal 'trafficking' [S2].
It requires manufacturers to provide tools needed to disable and reset electronic security locks, through a secure data release system if needed, so an independent shop can complete a repair [S2].

Enforcement is through the Federal Trade Commission, which would treat violations as unfair or deceptive practices under the FTC Act, and state attorneys general could sue for injunctions, civil penalties, restitution, and damages on behalf of state residents [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Powered wheelchair and mobility device manufacturers would bear the cost of sharing repair information and selling parts and diagnostic tools to independent shops on equal terms. Some manufacturers earn revenue from repairs performed only through authorized channels, and this would open that work to competition.

drawbacks.text: Manufacturers raise safety concerns: they argue that repairs by untrained technicians on devices that bear a person's weight could cause injury. The bill addresses this by shielding manufacturers from liability for damage caused by an independent repair or owner during repair, unless it stems from a design or manufacturing defect [S2].
The bill does not require manufacturers to sell a part that is no longer available, so owners of older devices could still be unable to obtain discontinued components [S2].

Manufacturers remain protected from having to divulge trade secrets, except as necessary to provide the repair materials the bill requires, which could leave room for disputes over what must be shared [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the people affected, the benefits are direct and personal: a powered wheelchair that sits broken for weeks while waiting for an authorized repair is a loss of mobility, work, and independence. The main costs fall on manufacturers, who would face new obligations to share repair information and compete for repair work. Good-faith safety concerns are partly answered by the liability provision and the requirement to provide lock-reset tools through secure channels, though disputes over what counts as a necessary repair tool would likely follow.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in the House in late August 2025 and referred to the Energy and Commerce and Judiciary committees; no hearing, markup, or vote has taken place, and Congress is still in session.

narrative.text: Rep. Maxwell Frost introduced the Wheelchair Right to Repair Act on August 26, 2025, with Rep. Sara Perez as the sole cosponsor [S1][S2][S3].
The bill was referred to the Committee on Energy and Commerce and, in addition, to the Committee on the Judiciary; no further action appears in the record [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, no one has gained or lost; manufacturers face no new obligations because the bill has not advanced.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No one yet; the bill sits in committee

sides.party_line_note: The bill has two Democratic sponsors and no Republican support in the record so far, though no vote has occurred to show where members stand.

industries.industry: Powered wheelchair and mobility device manufacturers
industries.note: The bill would require these manufacturers to share repair documentation, parts, software, and tools with independent shops and owners on terms equal to what they give authorized dealers, opening repair work to competition. Repair performed only through authorized channels is a revenue stream this bill would erode.

industries.industry: Independent repair shops and repair technicians
industries.note: Shops not affiliated with manufacturers would gain legal access to manuals, diagnostic software, parts, and lock-reset tools, letting them compete for wheelchair repair work. Their interest runs alongside the device owners they serve.

analysis.trajectory: With a single cosponsor and no recorded committee action two months after introduction, the bill is unlikely to advance in this Congress unless right-to-repair issues gain momentum or the sponsors build a broader coalition; the usual path for a bill at this stage is to die in committee at the end of the session.
